screens.title: Contract Instance: Address + ABI
screens.narratorSegment: A Contract instance in ethers. js is the runtime object that lets you call a deployed smart contract's functions and listen for events. It needs two things: the contract's address on the blockchain, and its ABI, the JSON description of the public interface. The address points to the deployed bytecode and storage; the ABI tells ethers. js how to encode function calls and decode return values. Concretely, Hardhat writes ABI data into artifacts/contracts/ContractName. sol/ContractName. json after compilation. You can either call ethers. getContractAt("ContractName", "0x... address...") which finds the ABI via Hardhat and returns a Contract, or construct one directly with new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signerOrProvider). For example, attaching to a Counter contract gives you methods like count(), increment(), and decrement() already typed and ready to call. A common misconception is thinking the ABI contains private keys or on-chain storage; it does not. The ABI is strictly a description for encoding calls. To summarize: address locates the contract, ABI describes its surface, and together they produce the Contract object you use in scripts and tasks. How would you verify you loaded the correct ABI for the deployed address?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Contract = address + ABI; use ethers.getContractAt or new ethers.Contract to create instances for interaction.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Contract Instance
What a Contract instance contains
Address locates the deployed code. ABI describes functions, events, and types. Signer or Provider determines read/write capabilities.
Example
Using a Counter contract, attaching yields callable methods like count(), increment(), and decrement().
Misconception
The ABI is not secret; it contains no private keys or state. It only describes the public surface for encoding and decoding.
Key Takeaway

A correct address and matching ABI are required for predictable interactions; mismatches lead to call failures or incorrect decoding.

Code snippets
// using Hardhat helper
const counter = await ethers.getContractAt("Counter", "0xDeployedAddress...");

// or directly with ABI
const contractABI = require("../artifacts/contracts/Counter.sol/Counter.json").abi;
const counter2 = new ethers.Contract("0xDeployedAddress...", contractABI, ethers.provider);
Check you loaded the right ABI
  • Confirm artifact path artifacts/contracts/<Name>.sol/<Name>.json
  • Match function names and parameter types with your Solidity source
  • Ensure address corresponds to the deployed network

screens.title: ABI and Hardhat Artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is the JSON description that tells ethers. js what functions, events, and types a contract exposes. Hardhat produces these ABIs during compilation and places them in artifacts/contracts/ContractName. sol/ContractName. json. Inside that file you'll find a field named abi which is the array you pass to new ethers. Contract(...) or use when calling getContractAt. In practice, you require or import the JSON file in a Node script to read the ABI. For example, require('../artifacts/contracts/Counter. sol/Counter. json'). abi gives you the ABI array for the compiled Counter. A common novice mistake is manually copying an ABI snippet from a block explorer that may not match the compiled bytecode or the exact version; prefer the artifact generated by your compile step. Also remember that ABIs don't include runtime storage state or private keys; they simply describe the interface. When writing scripts, load ABI programmatically from artifacts so your automation always uses the ABI derived from your current source code. How would you ensure your deployed address corresponds to the ABI you're loading? ABI and Hardhat Artifacts means hardhat artifacts contain abi json. load artifacts programmatically to avoid mismatches between code and abi.. In practical terms, where the abi lives and how to load it into scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › ABI & Artifacts
Where to find the ABI
Hardhat writes compiled artifacts with bytecode and ABI. Use artifacts path to load the ABI into scripts and tasks.
Code
// load ABI from Hardhat artifact
const artifact = require("../artifacts/contracts/Counter.sol/Counter.json");
const abi = artifact.abi;
const counter = new ethers.Contract(CONTRACT_ADDRESS, abi, ethers.provider);
Practical check
  • Confirm compile step completed before running scripts
  • Use the artifact from your project, not a copied ABI
  • Match the contract name and compiled output version
Why loading artifacts matters
Loading ABI from artifacts ensures your scripts target the exact interface your source compiled into. It avoids mismatches that lead to call failures or decoded values that make no sense.
Misconception
An ABI copy from elsewhere might mismatch parameter names or types; always prefer the project's compiled artifact to keep interface parity.
Try this

After compiling, open artifacts/.../Contract.json and inspect the abi array to confirm your expected functions exist before running a script against a deployed address.

screens.title: Provider vs Signer
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between a Provider and a Signer is central to safe contract interactions. A Provider is a read-only connection to the blockchain; it can fetch state and simulate view or pure function calls. These calls do not create transactions or cost gas. In contrast, a Signer represents an account that can sign and send transactions, change state, and spend Ether to pay for gas. For example, calling counter. count() through ethers. provider returns the current value without any gas. But calling counter. increment() requires a Signer: the transaction must be signed and mined, and your account will pay gas. A common trap is initializing a Contract with a Provider only and then attempting writes; ethers will throw or silently fail to sign. Another mistake is using a Signer but forgetting the correct network: the signer must connect to the same network where the contract is deployed. Practically, use Provider for reads in monitoring scripts and a Signer in scripts that perform state changes. Which interactions in your workflow truly need signing, and which can be done cheaply with a provider?

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Provider = read-only RPC access. Signer = account with private key for signing and paying gas. Use the right one for reads vs writes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Provider vs Signer
Provider
Connects to an RPC node for read-only queries. No signing and no gas expenditure.
Example
const counter = new ethers.Contract(addr, abi, ethers.provider); const current = await counter.count();
Misuse
Attempting a state-changing call with only a provider will fail because no signature or gas payment is provided.
Signer
Represents an account with a private key; can sign and send transactions and pay gas.
Example
const [signer] = await ethers.getSigners(); const counter = new ethers.Contract(addr, abi, signer); const tx = await counter.increment();
Pro tip

Use provider-based reads in monitoring tools to avoid unnecessary gas. Use signer for controlled writes, and always confirm the signer is on the correct network.

screens.title: Read-only Calls (view / pure)
screens.narratorSegment: Read-only function calls, marked view or pure in Solidity, are executed off-chain by the connected RPC node and do not produce transactions or cost gas. When you call such functions from ethers. js, the provider simulates the call and returns the result directly. For example, a public state variable like count in a Counter contract has an autogenerated getter. Calling const currentCount = await counter. count(); returns the numeric value immediately. Read calls are deterministic from the node's current view of the chain; they are useful for UI displays, monitoring scripts, and tests that assert state. A common misunderstanding is to expect a view call to create events or change state; it will not. If you need to know the exact on-chain state after a transaction, read again after awaiting the transaction receipt. In monitoring environments, choose a reliable provider endpoint and consider consistency: a read from a remote public RPC might be slightly stale compared to a local node. For practice, call count before and after sending a transaction to observe how reads reflect state changes once the transaction is mined.

keyIdea.text: view/pure functions run locally via the provider, return values immediately, and do not consume gas or change state.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Read-only Calls
Calling a view function
View and pure functions return data without creating a transaction. They use the provider for a local simulation.
// read a public state variable
const current = await counter.count();
console.log(`Current count: ${'${current.toString()}'}');
When to use reads
  • Displaying UI state
  • Running tests that assert values
  • Monitoring contract metrics
Misconceptions
A view call will never emit events or permanently change state. If you need to mutate state, you must send a transaction with a signer and await its confirmation.
Check your understanding

Call count() before and after a signed increment() transaction that you wait to confirm. Does the read reflect the updated state? Why or why not?

screens.title: Sending State-changing Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: State-changing functions produce transactions that modify blockchain state and cost gas. The process has three practical steps: prepare a Contract instance with a Signer, invoke the function to send the transaction, and await the transaction to be mined with tx. wait(). For example, to increment a Counter you connect a signer and call const tx = await counter. connect(signer). increment(); then const receipt = await tx. wait();. The first await returns a TransactionResponse containing the transaction hash, and the second await gives you the TransactionReceipt with block number, gas used, and any emitted events. A common pitfall is calling the function and not awaiting tx. wait(), which can lead to race conditions when subsequent logic expects the state change to be finalized. Another nuance: transactions may take time to mine depending on network congestion, so consider user feedback and retries in production scripts. Practice: always log both the TransactionResponse hash and the TransactionReceipt details so you can debug failures or confirm the change. Sending State-changing Transactions means send a signed transaction to change state; await tx.wait() to receive the receipt and confirm the change.. In practical terms, sign, send, and await transactions that modify contract state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transaction lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Send a signed transaction to change state; await tx.wait() to receive the receipt and confirm the change.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › State-changing Transactions
Three-step process
  1. Ensure Contract initialized with a Signer capable of paying gas.
  2. Send the transaction by calling the state-changing method.
  3. Await tx.wait() to obtain the TransactionReceipt and confirm the block inclusion.
// send and await
const tx = await counter.connect(signer).increment();
console.log('tx hash:', tx.hash);
const receipt = await tx.wait();
console.log('mined in block', receipt.blockNumber);
Why awaiting matters
Without awaiting the receipt, subsequent reads or dependent actions may observe the previous state and cause logic errors or failed assertions.
Common mistake
Not awaiting tx.wait() or assuming immediate finality. Always handle asynchronous confirmation and potential reorgs in robust systems.
Key Takeaway

A transaction response is only the submission. The receipt confirms the change and includes gas and event details important for verification.

screens.title: TransactionResponse vs TransactionReceipt
screens.narratorSegment: When you send a transaction via ethers. js you interact with two objects: the TransactionResponse returned immediately after sending, and the TransactionReceipt returned after the transaction is mined. The TransactionResponse gives you the transaction hash, the sender, and a promise you can later wait on; it's proof the transaction was submitted. The TransactionReceipt, returned by await tx. wait(), confirms the block, includes gasUsed, logs for emitted events, and the status field indicating success or failure. For example, when calling increment(), you get tx. hash from the response; after await tx. wait(), receipt. gasUsed and receipt. blockNumber tell you how expensive and when the transaction executed. A typical debugging workflow logs both objects: hash to track the transaction externally, and receipt to confirm events and gas. A common misconception is assuming the response alone is enough to assert a state change. It is not. Always await the receipt before reading state that depends on that transaction. How will you surface event logs from the receipt to validate contract behavior? TransactionResponse vs TransactionReceipt means transactionresponse = submission info and hash. transactionreceipt = mined confirmation with gas, block, and logs.. In practical terms, what each object represents and what useful fields they contain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Receipt vs Response
keyIdea.text: TransactionResponse = submission info and hash. TransactionReceipt = mined confirmation with gas, block, and logs.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Response vs Receipt
TransactionResponse
Returned immediately after sending a transaction. Contains the hash and a promise to wait for the receipt.
const tx = await counter.increment();
console.log(tx.hash);
// tx is a TransactionResponse
TransactionReceipt
Returned after await tx.wait(); includes gasUsed, blockNumber, and logs with emitted events for validation.
const receipt = await tx.wait();
console.log(receipt.blockNumber, receipt.gasUsed);
console.log(receipt.logs); // event data
Debugging tip
Log the tx.hash for explorer lookup and inspect receipt.logs to confirm expected events emitted by your contract.

screens.title: Sending ETH and Payable Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Sending Ether to a contract can be done in two ways: calling a payable function with a value override, or sending a raw transaction to the contract address. If your contract has a payable function like deposit(), include an overrides object with value when calling it, for example await contract. deposit({ value: ethers. utils. parseEther('0.1') });. Alternatively, use the signer to send a simple transaction to the contract address: await signer. sendTransaction({ to: contractAddress, value: ethers. utils. parseEther('0.5') });. Both operations consume gas and must be signed by an account with sufficient Ether. A common mistake is forgetting to convert Ether units; use ethers. utils. parseEther to convert decimal strings to wei. Another mistake is assuming a provider can send Ether; sending requires a Signer. After the transaction is mined, inspect the TransactionReceipt to confirm the transfer and any contract-side effects. Practically, use payable function calls when you want the contract to react to the funds in a specific way, and sendTransaction for simple funding. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Interact Script
Example script
This script reads the Counter, increments, waits, then decrements and confirms each change.
// scripts/interact_counter.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const CONTRACT_ADDRESS = "YOUR_DEPLOYED_COUNTER_ADDRESS"; // replace
  const [signer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  const CounterFactory = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
  const counter = CounterFactory.attach(CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

  console.log("--- Initial State ---");
  let currentCount = await counter.count();
  console.log(`Current count: ${'${currentCount.toString()}'}');

  console.log("--- Incrementing Counter ---");
  const incTx = await counter.connect(signer).increment();
  await incTx.wait();
  console.log("Increment transaction successful!");

  currentCount = await counter.count();
  console.log(`New count: ${'${currentCount.toString()}'}');
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
Run it
npx hardhat run scripts/interact_counter.js --network sepolia

screens.title: Hardhat Tasks for Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat tasks let you package interaction logic into reusable CLI commands. You define tasks in hardhat. config. js or separate files and include parameters so you can pass a contract address or network at runtime. The example task increment-counter registers a parameter contract and then performs an attach, reads the current count, calls increment, awaits the transaction, and prints the new count. Tasks are great for repeated operations like maintenance scripts or QA flows because they reduce friction and human error. When defining a task, you typically get signers via ethers. getSigners(), fetch the contract factory, attach to the address, and call the intended methods. Always ensure the network flag matches the deployment network when running tasks, because running a task on the wrong network can have no effect or cause unexpected transactions. Tasks also let you chain operations and include safe guards like confirmations, dry-run flags, or gas limit checks. After creating tasks, running npx hardhat increment-counter --contract --network sepolia executes a scripted, repeatable interaction with clear logging. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Hardhat Tasks
Define a task
Tasks accept params and run code inside the Hardhat runtime. They are ideal for CLI-driven automation.
// hardhat.config.js or tasks/increment.js
task("increment-counter", "Increments the Counter contract")
  .addParam("contract", "The Counter contract address")
  .setAction(async (taskArgs) => {
    const [signer] = await ethers.getSigners();
    const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    const counter = Counter.attach(taskArgs.contract);

    console.log("Current count:", (await counter.count()).toString());
    const tx = await counter.connect(signer).increment();
    await tx.wait();
    console.log("Incremented! New count:", (await counter.count()).toString());
  });
Run
npx hardhat increment-counter --contract <address> --network sepolia

screens.title: Common Errors and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: When interacting with deployed contracts, a few recurring errors account for most problems. First, forgetting to connect a Signer for state-changing functions causes failures—ensure counter. connect(signer) or initialize the Contract with a signer. Second, not awaiting tx. wait() produces race conditions where subsequent reads show stale state; always await the receipt before continuing. Third, using the wrong ABI or the wrong deployed address leads to function not found errors or incorrect decoding; prefer the local artifact ABI and verify the address against your deployment record. Fourth, running scripts against the wrong network (for example using a sepolia RPC while the contract is on localhost) will either throw or silently do nothing—confirm the Hardhat network flag matches the deployment network. Finally, unit mistakes such as forgetting to use ethers. utils. parseEther for value fields can send incorrect amounts. The defensive workflow: log tx. hash, await receipt, confirm blockNumber and gasUsed, and verify event logs. Practically, add clear console output and error handling in scripts to speed debugging. Which of these checks will you add to your automation pipeline first? Common Errors and Debugging means always confirm signer presence, await tx.wait(), match abi and address, use correct network, and convert ether units properly.. In practical terms, diagnose signer issues, await mistakes, abi/address mismatches, and network problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to pick up a deployed contract and use ethers. js and Hardhat to read its state, send transactions, and automate common interactions. We focus on two essential pieces: the contract's address and its ABI, because together they let ethers. js encode and decode calls correctly. You'll see how read-only calls use a provider and cost no gas, while state-changing calls require a signer and produce a transaction that must be awaited until it is mined. We'll walk through practical examples using a simple Counter contract: reading the count, incrementing and decrementing via signed transactions, and sending ETH to payable functions. We'll also cover creating scripts and Hardhat tasks so you can run common operations from the CLI, and point out frequent mistakes like forgetting to connect a signer or not awaiting tx. wait(). By the end you'll be able to instantiate Contract objects, perform safe reads and writes, and automate those interactions with scripts and tasks. Ready to connect to a deployed contract and work with it reliably?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a Contract instance for an already deployed contract, call its read-only functions without spending gas, and send state-changing transactions that require signing and gas payment. You will also understand where Hardhat stores ABI artifacts and how to load them into scripts, how to send ETH to payable functions or to a contract address directly, and how to wrap common interactions into Hardhat tasks. These are practical skills: for example, you'll write a script that reads a Counter's count, submits an increment transaction, waits for confirmation, and then reads the new count to verify the change. We'll also practice diagnosing common errors, such as using a provider when a signer is required, or forgetting to await tx. wait(), which can lead to race conditions. Each objective emphasizes a concrete task and why it matters for reliable deployment and automation.

These secondary objectives focus on practical steps: locate the ABI compiled by Hardhat, choose between ethers. getContractAt and Contract. attach, and correctly configure signer or provider in scripts. You'll practice sending ETH to a contract address and to a payable function, and learn to interpret TransactionResponse and TransactionReceipt objects to confirm that changes occurred. We also emphasize debugging techniques: verifying the network matches the deployment network, ensuring your contract address matches the deployed address, and checking the ABI matches the compiled contract. Together these skills build a reliable interaction workflow so your scripts behave predictably across localhost, testnets, and mainnet. You'll know not just what commands to run, but why each step is necessary and how to recover from common pitfalls. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means hands-on abilities: find abi, attach to a contract, use signer/provider correctly, send eth, and validate transactions with receipts.. In practical terms, concrete tasks you'll perform in the lab. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Contract instance in ethers. js is the runtime object that lets you call a deployed smart contract's functions and listen for events. It needs two things: the contract's address on the blockchain, and its ABI, the JSON description of the public interface. The address points to the deployed bytecode and storage; the ABI tells ethers. js how to encode function calls and decode return values. Concretely, Hardhat writes ABI data into artifacts/contracts/ContractName. sol/ContractName. json after compilation. You can either call ethers. getContractAt("ContractName", "0x... address...") which finds the ABI via Hardhat and returns a Contract, or construct one directly with new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signerOrProvider). For example, attaching to a Counter contract gives you methods like count(), increment(), and decrement() already typed and ready to call. A common misconception is thinking the ABI contains private keys or on-chain storage; it does not. The ABI is strictly a description for encoding calls. To summarize: address locates the contract, ABI describes its surface, and together they produce the Contract object you use in scripts and tasks. How would you verify you loaded the correct ABI for the deployed address?

The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is the JSON description that tells ethers. js what functions, events, and types a contract exposes. Hardhat produces these ABIs during compilation and places them in artifacts/contracts/ContractName. sol/ContractName. json. Inside that file you'll find a field named abi which is the array you pass to new ethers. Contract(...) or use when calling getContractAt. In practice, you require or import the JSON file in a Node script to read the ABI. For example, require('../artifacts/contracts/Counter. sol/Counter. json'). abi gives you the ABI array for the compiled Counter. A common novice mistake is manually copying an ABI snippet from a block explorer that may not match the compiled bytecode or the exact version; prefer the artifact generated by your compile step. Also remember that ABIs don't include runtime storage state or private keys; they simply describe the interface. When writing scripts, load ABI programmatically from artifacts so your automation always uses the ABI derived from your current source code. How would you ensure your deployed address corresponds to the ABI you're loading? ABI and Hardhat Artifacts means hardhat artifacts contain abi json. load artifacts programmatically to avoid mismatches between code and abi.. In practical terms, where the abi lives and how to load it into scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the difference between a Provider and a Signer is central to safe contract interactions. A Provider is a read-only connection to the blockchain; it can fetch state and simulate view or pure function calls. These calls do not create transactions or cost gas. In contrast, a Signer represents an account that can sign and send transactions, change state, and spend Ether to pay for gas. For example, calling counter. count() through ethers. provider returns the current value without any gas. But calling counter. increment() requires a Signer: the transaction must be signed and mined, and your account will pay gas. A common trap is initializing a Contract with a Provider only and then attempting writes; ethers will throw or silently fail to sign. Another mistake is using a Signer but forgetting the correct network: the signer must connect to the same network where the contract is deployed. Practically, use Provider for reads in monitoring scripts and a Signer in scripts that perform state changes. Which interactions in your workflow truly need signing, and which can be done cheaply with a provider?

Read-only function calls, marked view or pure in Solidity, are executed off-chain by the connected RPC node and do not produce transactions or cost gas. When you call such functions from ethers. js, the provider simulates the call and returns the result directly. For example, a public state variable like count in a Counter contract has an autogenerated getter. Calling const currentCount = await counter. count(); returns the numeric value immediately. Read calls are deterministic from the node's current view of the chain; they are useful for UI displays, monitoring scripts, and tests that assert state. A common misunderstanding is to expect a view call to create events or change state; it will not. If you need to know the exact on-chain state after a transaction, read again after awaiting the transaction receipt. In monitoring environments, choose a reliable provider endpoint and consider consistency: a read from a remote public RPC might be slightly stale compared to a local node. For practice, call count before and after sending a transaction to observe how reads reflect state changes once the transaction is mined.

State-changing functions produce transactions that modify blockchain state and cost gas. The process has three practical steps: prepare a Contract instance with a Signer, invoke the function to send the transaction, and await the transaction to be mined with tx. wait(). For example, to increment a Counter you connect a signer and call const tx = await counter. connect(signer). increment(); then const receipt = await tx. wait();. The first await returns a TransactionResponse containing the transaction hash, and the second await gives you the TransactionReceipt with block number, gas used, and any emitted events. A common pitfall is calling the function and not awaiting tx. wait(), which can lead to race conditions when subsequent logic expects the state change to be finalized. Another nuance: transactions may take time to mine depending on network congestion, so consider user feedback and retries in production scripts. Practice: always log both the TransactionResponse hash and the TransactionReceipt details so you can debug failures or confirm the change. Sending State-changing Transactions means send a signed transaction to change state; await tx.wait() to receive the receipt and confirm the change.. In practical terms, sign, send, and await transactions that modify contract state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you send a transaction via ethers. js you interact with two objects: the TransactionResponse returned immediately after sending, and the TransactionReceipt returned after the transaction is mined. The TransactionResponse gives you the transaction hash, the sender, and a promise you can later wait on; it's proof the transaction was submitted. The TransactionReceipt, returned by await tx. wait(), confirms the block, includes gasUsed, logs for emitted events, and the status field indicating success or failure. For example, when calling increment(), you get tx. hash from the response; after await tx. wait(), receipt. gasUsed and receipt. blockNumber tell you how expensive and when the transaction executed. A typical debugging workflow logs both objects: hash to track the transaction externally, and receipt to confirm events and gas. A common misconception is assuming the response alone is enough to assert a state change. It is not. Always await the receipt before reading state that depends on that transaction. Sending Ether to a contract can be done in two ways: calling a payable function with a value override, or sending a raw transaction to the contract address. If your contract has a payable function like deposit(), include an overrides object with value when calling it, for example await contract. deposit({ value: ethers. utils. parseEther('0.1') });. Alternatively, use the signer to send a simple transaction to the contract address: await signer. sendTransaction({ to: contractAddress, value: ethers. utils. parseEther('0.5') });. Both operations consume gas and must be signed by an account with sufficient Ether. A common mistake is forgetting to convert Ether units; use ethers. utils. parseEther to convert decimal strings to wei. Another mistake is assuming a provider can send Ether; sending requires a Signer. After the transaction is mined, inspect the TransactionReceipt to confirm the transfer and any contract-side effects. Practically, use payable function calls when you want the contract to react to the funds in a specific way, and sendTransaction for simple funding. Hardhat tasks let you package interaction logic into reusable CLI commands. When interacting with deployed contracts, a few recurring errors account for most problems. First, forgetting to connect a Signer for state-changing functions causes failures—ensure counter. connect(signer) or initialize the Contract with a signer. Second, not awaiting tx. wait() produces race conditions where subsequent reads show stale state; always await the receipt before continuing. Third, using the wrong ABI or the wrong deployed address leads to function not found errors or incorrect decoding; prefer the local artifact ABI and verify the address against your deployment record. Fourth, running scripts against the wrong network (for example using a sepolia RPC while the contract is on localhost) will either throw or silently do nothing—confirm the Hardhat network flag matches the deployment network. Finally, unit mistakes such as forgetting to use ethers. utils. parseEther for value fields can send incorrect amounts. The defensive workflow: log tx. hash, await receipt, confirm blockNumber and gasUsed, and verify event logs. Practically, add clear console output and error handling in scripts to speed debugging. To make your interactions reliable, adopt a few best practices. First, centralize configuration: keep deployment addresses, network endpoints, and artifact paths in a shared config so scripts and tasks reference the same sources. Second, always compile before running interaction scripts to ensure the ABI matches the deployed bytecode. Third, in scripts and tasks explicitly obtain signers and confirm their addresses and networks at runtime before sending transactions. Fourth, log transaction hashes and inspect receipts for gasUsed and events; this helps post-run verification. Fifth, build idempotent tasks or include dry-run and confirmation flags so maintenance operations can be previewed safely. Finally, consider waiting for multiple confirmations for critical flows or listening for specific events to ensure the state change you expect indeed occurred.
